newsitem.title: GERMANY: D.Telekom faces new regulatory challenges.
newsitem.headline: D.Telekom faces new regulatory challenges.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG, the German phone giant, is under increasing pressure as a gathering storm of protest from competitors looks set to explode into a regulatory battle.

Sounding the charge was an impatient executive from Mannesmann AG, the German industry and technology group, who threatened to file a formal complaint with state regulators unless Telekom quickly granted rivals access to its network.

Peter Mihatsch, Mannesmann board member, accused Telekom of delaying tactics and demanding prices for allowing competitors to connect to its network that were "as much as 10 times" the levels charged in Britain, the U.S. or proposed fees in France.
"Our patience is not eternal," Mihatsch told a news conference at the CeBIT technology trade fair in Hanover.
"This is now a question of weeks if not days. We will first go to the Post and Telecommunications Ministry," he added.

Deutsche Telekom is the only phone company in Germany with a comprehensive communications network that reaches into every road and byway, with some 40 million phone lines connecting residential customers and millions of businesses.

New competitors, who have patchy networks, must either lease lines from Telekom to gain access to customers or find some other way to cross the last mile from their telephone exchanges to the customer's door.

Called interconnection in industry jargon, it usually means that a telephone company buys access to another company's network at wholesale prices and covers these costs by charging higher retail prices to its own customers.

The level of interconnection fees and the terms of interconnection are seen by many of Telekom's rivals as the single issue that could make or break Germany's efforts to open the sector to full-blown competition next year.
Klaus-Dieter Scheuerle, a senior regulatory official in the postal ministry, said it was only a matter of time before the first complaints demanding regulatory action began rolling in.
"Actually, I consider it astounding that they have waited so long," he told reporters on the sidelines of the fair.
Should Telekom fail to strike an interconnection agreement and one of its rivals files a complaint, the government regulator has 10 weeks to review the matter and decide.
Scheuerle said Telekom was currently involved in interconnection negotiations with over 20 separate companies.

He said the government was currently studying interconnection rules and fees in other countries and would use these to create a theoretical example of a "comparative market" which it will use to judge the fairness of the fees that Telekom is planning to charge its rivals.
"We will probably end up in a situation where Telekom does not provide us with a detailed cost analysis," he said.

In that case, the ministry will determine whether Telekom should be made to lower fees to levels comparable to those charged in the United States or Britain, which Telekom has until now said would be unfair.
"We do not share Telekom's statements that the United States should not serve as a comparable market," he said.
Deutsche Telekom chairman Ron Sommer said this week that he was prepared to reach an interconnection deal and believed that rivals were just "already looking for an excuse to explain their failure".
He said the company had struck such an agreement with WorldCom, the U.S. business communications group that is expanding rapidly in Europe. But this has not been independently confirmed.
Scheuerle said he has also heard about the deal but does not know any details. The government must give final approval for it to take effect.
"We have written to Telekom and asked for a copy of the agreement," he said.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
